Editor’s Note

Bob Randolph can be blunt, transparent and charming. His passions explode here and mark them. His poetry is accessible.

Bob can be loving, spontaneous, ridiculous, demanding, self-absorbed, brilliantly creative, funny, generous, insightful, obsessive… and driven.

He was one of the last Americans called before the House Committee on Un-American Activities for refusing to sign a “loyalty oath” at the University of California. He was at the Bay of Pigs a week before the CIA-sponsored invasion. He visited the Soviet Bloc under Communism, to see for himself. He is a WWII U.S. Army veteran, a human-rights advocate, a friend to underdogs, the downtrodden, animals, trees and the planet.

This book was made possible by the indispensable help and encouragement of Harold Murphree. It is dedicated to his memory. Thanks also to Clay Kempf for technical assistance.

— Mark Wotton, Editor
Introduction
by Tom Sanders

For forty-five years Bob Randolph and I have discussed almost every subject under the sun that good friends talk about, but it was only when he became a full-time poet that I realized that I had really never known him.

By reading his many poems, I discovered that he saw a beauty in sorrow, in death and in work that others are blind to. I discovered that Ecclesiastes was wrong — that there is something new under the sun: Bob Randolph’s poetry.

His poems tell the truth he sees and feels, and he sees where others are blind and feels where others are callous. He even closes his eyes sometimes in order to see better. He questions authority, himself and everything that should be questioned.

All of his poems have their roots in the earth and have a foundation in reality, because the poison of the cities has never polluted his heart.

For Bob Randolph, there are no candles like the stars, no altars like the mountains, no preachers like the common people. For inspiration he needs only to mingle with people. It is by the light of these lives that he writes. He sees the universe as kindly, and all that lives emerges and then returns to that kindness.

— Tom Sanders, Unitarian minister, journalist, poet · 17 December 2008
Preface

Okay, here I am, 89 years old and now what? Well, it depends on how much distance we can give our observations. The distance to God’s toilet, where he goes to sit and do his best thinking.

From there we are seen as an absolutely monstrous species, feeling free to kill any and all creatures, including our own. Our media can lie to whatever extent is needed, trust me.

I am about to put out thoughts to whomever, about what each of us should be planning to do within this crisis — the crisis the power structure is incapable of seeing honestly.

— Bob Randolph
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The nature of matter
Matter exists at sub-atomic levels where it doesn't weigh anything but is just a particle of plus or minus, a tiny field of force that is not measurable that is not matter but is matter eventually that can weigh billions of tons per star. Somehow I think these mysteries matter very much.
July 11, 1997
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Dialectics
Water will boil at 212 degrees Fahrenheit, following the dictionary definition of dialectics - when quantitative change goes far enough it will switch to qualitative change. It will have no choice, it must do this. It cannot stay liquid, it must boil. When oppression reaches 212 degrees Fahrenheit the masses will boil. They are following an immutable law of nature, wisely created by the gods.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
A baby bird between air and breath
Not every life is lived. Some are hatched and live naked in the nest for a few days, learning how to hold its little head up and desperately learning how to open its little beak, its tiny yellow beak, its upper and lower beak it must learn to open just hours out of the egg. Just hours, and the world is huge and very cool and the sky is huge and the most precious thing this little bird owns is its beak -- for that is how it will have a chance to live. And so all these babies that are not yet fully babies, but barely dwell between air and breath, between gentle rain at night and the beginning of blood between worlds. And on that day this tiny spirit rested in my hand, this baby bird, naked with its lovely perfect two-lipped beak in its little body that flickered on because two parent birds mated, and flickered out because a tiny catastrophe pushed it over the edge in a heart-breaking instant. During the remaining 20 years of mine, I will remember this darling whose life ended when it began, whose love ended, whose dream of life ended -- and is now in me, to tell its story in all the seasons, in all the phases of the moon in all the chapels, all the gardens, and on all the windy slopes where life struggles to survive -- for a while.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Flaws
An emerald's beauty comes from flaws, a hint of something gone awry in all the axes of its gorgeous green. Amethyst, crystal-faced with lavendar light makes quartz more than itself. All so because distemper taints a rocky little soul deep down within itself. Disordered atoms give a gentle smoke-like hue to simple quartz— so richly seen because it's tinged with pain. The topaz, yellow, brown translucent light, so wrought by form that twists and writhes before our eyes; so pure an amber flash that weeps within itself. come to light as ruby— or sapphire, to yield at last such god-like rose or blue, so softly starred upon our hand. The diamond's poverty of color— its soul is only on a cutting edge, where sudden light cries out in blue and red and mauve… to tell us more of broken hopes, of laughter stabbing on a knife-like edge to ease some inner cry. All these are teachers for us now So fixed in time and space, their beauty shaped in fever heat— locked in a longer time than we. January, 1987
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
God is the space between plus and minus
Miracles everywhere - the spiral shapes of galaxies, some bar-shaped double spirals, perhaps with no life, some with water but no life, some with water and life - Miracles everywhere, the wonder of the wings and eyes and legs of ordinary house flies, the even greater wonder of the creations of the universe's finest architects, garden spiders, with their great silver lacy delicate web wheels meant to capture miraculous house flies with their wondrously made eyes and wings and legs and nervous systems, to be simple food like out of a can, with no caring whatever by the spider - hungry because without food for 6 days - for the wonders of the design of the house fly, all miracles, made by whatever, some call it God, or not made by anything, just another version of the way plus and minus play themselves out in creation. The alligators, man-eating sharks, hydrogen bombs, plutonium oxide, the most toxic substance in the universe, all made by magic, the magic of polarity, the magic of gravity, the magic of chance, the magic of events, the magic of light waves that do not disappear at a distance, of sound waves that do disappear at a distance, of radiation waves of a thousand frequencies - of trillions of opposites - that somehow the most compelling space is that between plus and minus, between protons and electrons, between stars and planets, between planets and moons, in the great yet tiny spaces between the 17 separate galaxies of our "local group", only barely relevant in the unfolding vastness, the neutral charge of empty space between the plus and minus charges the neutral charge of empty space between the plus and minus charges of life and earth and clouds and sky and male minus and female plus, of eggs, of ova and sperm - all thought up by nothing at all, for if a god or gods created it all then they would show cruelty as their creations ate each other. Yes, all the miracles of every size, every color, every direction, all - all existing in the space between plus and minus, where if there's a god it must be here, it can only be here. It is at the least certainly not in sacred scriptures drawn up for ourselves, for only - only - only for our one species. No, the universe neither thinks nor is it mindless in any way other than with magic.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Minus One
When the lightning flashes with the earth, the tale we're told is that the sky is minus one. When my heart can pound and skip a beat, the tale I'm told is that my life is minus one. When I go to sleep and only dream of you, my spirit knows my night is minus one. The sound of minus one the feel of minus one the pulse of minus one the time of minus one Minus one Minus one To find the balance of my life is minus one Oh, tell my heart to hold me tight to light my pain of minus one. When laughter in the night can fill the vessels of our lives can take us deeply in its arms and let us see we're minus one. Across the mountains near the dawn A coyote's cry now seeking for his mate conveys the sound of minus one A yellow flower opening wide beneath the morning sun is reaching out for pollinating life to fill and still its minus one. The nursing baby the puppy or the cub, that cry for milk as best they can instinctively know the time has come to fill its minus one. My heart can break for minus one. The great elm spreading tall each yellow leaf will fall in its own turn, telling others thay are minus one. the best of minus one the pulse of minus one the life of minus one the death of minus one tha last love of minus one the first love of minus one so few condors left to soar on 8 foot wings, their nearing end caused by man's embrace of earth and air, this whole specie now nearly minus one. ancient minus one newborn minus one cloud shapes minus one minus one has been the key to understand for each end each death each season come and gone all change all life all time all are the sum of minus one yet for each lack each loss of minus one there are newer ones in their turn and time, that for now and eternally are a gain of one, the triumphant birth of one, the fertile time of one, let each time of minus one be rhythm's turn to keep it whole delicately balanced delicately poised at one and one and minus one, the womb is filled and when the babe is born, the mother finds herself feeling the loss of minus one
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
A one-legged blackbird
doesn't have any self-pity, and furthermore he or she can balance pretty good a twig up in the tree.
January 6, 2000
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The fish can't see the water
That's how you get used to something. You look at things as you swim around. It always looks the same, except at night, when it gets opaque gray with pollution, but after a while that's your world. Air is like water. We swim in it, like fish swim in water. We do not see the air. Fish do not see the water. We are told some things are true. We do not know that - we are only told it. We do not see them, or know where they come from, we do not see the air, fish do not see the water. If water is polluted when fish are born, it looks like the truth to them. That's the only way they know it. When we are born into poisoned air, we do not see it. It is all we know, it looks like the truth. Fish do not see the water. We do not see the air. We live and die in air and water we do not see.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The average head of cattle
The average head of cattle pretty much eats all the time. It eats grass on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I call it "it" because if it was once male it has had its balls lopped off and if it was female it has been defiled in some similar way. Next Wednesday at 3:15 pm it will be eating grass. At a quarter to six and also at a quarter to eleven it will be eating grass. All January it will be standing around - mostly, during the freezing nights wondering ever so slightly why it is so cold. Next March it will be eating grass on Mondays and Fridays, and also the rest of the week. During the first 30 days of September I suppose it will be eating grass. Then one day it will go over somewhere on a truck to a big building where it will have its brains smashed in - just like that. Wouldn't you imagine that by this time at least one cattle would look around a little thoughtfully at its fellows before it is too late, and say "Hey, does anybody here have any idea what this is all about?"
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
In silence
The wolf, the mountain lion, the eagle and the salmon are watching us. Don't ask them how they know. They just do. They know things are different, and they'll disappear in silence as every disappearing species has left the earth - in silence. . . . .
January 25, 1991
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The noble mold
The noble mold on German white grapes, or Hungarian Tokays, leaving them discolored, an odor of rot, like stale unwashed clothing. yet sheltered within the chemistries are all the derivative liquids of lives of older ones; of grapes or souls, at last touching the threshold of a nectared myrrh, delicately poised a time before their death, to give a liquid perfume so ethereal and sweetly dear it can only be harvested in the immediate hours before their deaths, like the blended vintage lives of our elders - at the very last yielding up the perfect sense of life - seen only at this harvest time of gently dying lives, of grapes, of rotting fruit - of sweetly fermenting lives the time of life that is that richest, loveliest magic gift that must contain this mold of age - to let us have the richest sip of life, occurring only in the ripest time , the time of twinkling eyes underneath our shaggy brows and wrinkled cheeks so like the vines along the Danube and the Rhine, in the season of colored leaves so green and gray and orange and red - in the last days before the time of winter's silence - this noble mold must be earned, through the spring and the summertime, through the chilling dawns of autumn, to give us near the end those gorgeous spatlese, auslese, beerenauslese and trockenbeerenauslese wines - - summing up our lives.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Bordeaux wine
(The world-famous wines of France's Bordeaux region are as they are precisely because the soil is so poor.) Squeezed drop by drop from little rooted veins among the stones in this poor soil, craving with parched tongues, thirsting for the slightest moisture, sucking invisibly, gasping to last another hour - Yet tiny moisture by tiny drop, the button green grapes swell so slightly, with such effort, darkening and swelling like bruises - internal hemorraging lets bloody juices in this suckling fruit. The leaves, thin and gray, searching for shade to escape the heat; their poverty giving so little to the moisture in the stems. Yet....little by little, through the dry days, through the thirsty fields, the meager juice of wretched soil collects until in some Merlin's loving hands this painful juice is bottled, and shelved - to germinate and incubate and fester and grow old, and one day splash softly in our glass, drawn from these rocky pebbles of the Medoc, that starved those vines to greatness.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Manzanita
You wild dancers, you sinewy snakes weaving with intoxicated curiosity to see just who's around in this thousandth year of yours. Your dead wood, so firm like agate, with the lines of life of rhythms, cycles in your growth like the agate like jasper chalcedony and chert who all seem silent but are merely pictures at rest for the moment we gaze at them. These manzanita sisters, dancing wild sensuous lives on hot dry slopes. You manzanita your silky maroon forearms, your silky soft thighs, your vaginas where your limbs combine you devils that now at last can bring sanity to our frozen lives to free us to stir our bodies, minds and spirits together like a swirling batter for a wondrous marble cake of consciousness. Oh, manzanita, you manzanita sisters, stay with us, and if you dance away at night or just at dawn, remember us and know that we too have now absorbed your hardy love of life, that we too will flourish even with but 10 drops of water. We will dance all night to ancient songs both yours and ours and you and we, will think of one another at night and in the day and know our buds and seeds will spring anew to life on any slope, to tell the world and air to stay and see the sacred dance of you and me that only comes to rest when someone gazes in the eyes of you, a manzanita tree, a tree designed to help us humans see and be, with deep-set roots - like you, a manzanita tree.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
We are the weeds of the world
We have no pedigrees, we do not have shapely leaves or lavender flowers. We do not have classic features. We appear where we are not wanted and are an embarrassment to those who appreciate beauty and sip aperitifs in the late afternoon. We appear in the cracks in sidewalks and sometimes if allowed to be there too long we can crack the pavements of civilized societies. We grow in garbage dumps, in sewer ventilators, in the urinals of the rich, our thorny vines crawl from bidets across dressing tables toward fluorescent lights buried in black ceilings. We are ragged and unkempt but we are suited to wild storms offshore that flay our leaves with wind and wet sand, that would tear hothouse flowers to shreds. We can endure earthquakes because we are not in flower pots. We know gulls and geese and gray seas at dawn, we watch seals past the surf at daybreak, we thirst for water so our roots sink deeper in the dunes. We are the weeds of the world, native in every lush or forbidding place, without attention from sprinkling cans or compost spreaders. We cling to alpine crags and pry loose great boulders to fall each century changing forever the face of the earth, a power unknown to roses and daffodils. The weeds of the world can cover wartime's landscapes with soft green, can cover tombs of generals and dictators with dark green vines that call to insects with tiny flowers, to renew it all again - without end.. We are the weeds of the world.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
I am also my little dog Tidbit
Tidbit was running on the fast side of the road, between the Berkeley pier and the town He seemed so sure of himself his litle short legs, his fast stride, as though he knew something important already he seemed dear, and I wanted to know him I moved toward him, to pick him up and hold him for a moment, he was suddenly like all the puppies I had known when I was a boy. I held him in my arms Already there was two of us I said I would keep him til I found a good home for him. That's what I said, something I told myself but time began to pass I had found a little dish for him and I bought 3 cans for him . . . . just for the moment we were together but just a day at a time He had looked good, like he had lived with someone but he needed a collar and a name and now it seemed - we were living together? and this lovely little dark furry Lhasa Apso from Tibet, his bright little dark eyes, he needed a name and a collar, and already he was sleeping with me . . And we were going for walks and it was lovely already, we were knowing each other, a little the vet said "maybe 3 years old". But see, was he abandoned by the pier by someone who did not understand his little spirit? how he flourished with our love And with his little Tibetan ears hanging down like a spaniel's the comments from pssersbys during the 15 years since, "oh what a dear little fellow" and what that has meant to me during the 15 years he lived with me I felt such love for this new precious friend, such pride, a little fellow but a Lhasa Apso from Tibet!, clear around the world from where we are now! I walk him 3 times a day, and every time it feels like we're on a special parade! I'm so lucky to be his companion. He's my little dog, he will never be anyone else's! So this was the beginning in the world of wars in the middle east and elsewhere, of political powers at work, of great and fearful world events, but somehow, the things in our lives and with our dear Tidbit, we were closer to the center of life, to all its mysteries and miracles, to the patterns of love that matter in our lives, like kittens playing with a ball of yarn, like the smiles of babies, like the silences and sounds of nature on its shores and in its forests, like brief tendernesses in our own lives, kisses thrown to others everywhere, like every day shared with our dear little Tidbit from Tibet - from the other side of the world. I will remember most what I learned from him, how he always tried, during his partial blindness, during his infirmities, he always tried, he always sought to be alive, functioning, trying, reaching for everything in his little life. His life was not little to him, it was a complete life, it was his to live. This I learned from him, though I am older, what he has taught me I will remember as long as I live. From our precious Tidbit, that we will remember for the rest of our lives.
December 31, 2005
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Notice in Florida to birds flying south
You are advised to avoid Cuba, the island 90 miles from here, the former pearl of the Antilles. It will appear beautiful and welcome as a landfall, but you are advised to overfly it to Jamaica; in order to avoid its very detrimental communistic atmospheres and non-exclusive feeding and resting grounds where you may find yourself in the company of Cuban birds of most dubious persuasions.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
An island off the coast of Italy
In every sweetheart's dream, there is an island off the coast of Italy. Every shorebird has memories that echoed from an island off the coast of Italy. On the edge of every sunset on any ocean, there is such an island, and on the planet Venus long long ago, there was an island off the coast of Italy. In Casseoipeia, Andromeda, Cygnus the Swan and Ursa Major, there have been other islands off the coasts of other Italies. In my heart, even now that I am older, there will always be one, as the warm love I feel for you once swirled near birds' nests high on cliffs on an island off the coast of Italy. On the bleak chill coasts of Wales, Norway and Greenland, old men and old women have never seen an island off the coast of Italy, but they have dreamed of it gazing into the foam of their ale. Most of those who were born on an island off the coast of Italy are buried there, in a windswept graveyard that basks in the Mediterranean sun on summer days. An island off the coast of Italy is a place of living cliffs and green slopes, that still cannot believe it has that rare good fortune to be one of the islands off the coast of Italy.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The accumulation of capital
Capitalism is built on the most rapid possible accumulation of capital. Human well-being is based on the most patient delicate tender steady imaginative accumulation of love. Capital is the machinery, the factory buildings, the security guards, the steel and iron and marble and concrete, the jagged edges, the metal powder in the air, the rust in the gutters, the two inch wide supplies, the 4000 pound supplies, the 4 million screws, the plastic parts that won't rot but will crack, the foam rubber parts that won't crack but will rot, all this to take precedence over human laughter, body fluids and church choirs, precedence over backpacking on wild trails overlooking oceans, with soaring birds overhead, with small mammals surviving in the tall grass and watching us precedence over backpacking on wild trails carefully. But do not forget, whatever you do, if you want to be able to make your mortgage payments and buy liquor for your office parties, remember that power and employment are based on the most rapid possible accumulation of capital -- of the spread of concrete, plastic and laser beams, and have nothing to do with soft skin, eyelashes and tender lips.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The Rocks Along the Shore
The rocks along the shore laugh at the sea - until they are gone.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
Sailing into the wind
(Identical to the Book IV poem of the same title, p.175 — a deliberate reprise.) When we know how to trim the sails we can sail into the wind. The leading edge of our will can cleave a narrow path into winds that howl and divert their fury into turbulence that circles, billowing our sails, and our lives - and let us defy and harness raw nature herself.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
A Clothesline Between Galaxies
I know. It's never been done before. But if an ordinary rope was spun as fine as the finest silky spider web it might reach. Let's just say it reaches. We'll attach it here and the other end on some kind of a stick on some small planet in Andromeda where there's life - at least where there's a stick. Yet that great depth of space - 2,000 000 light years and yet Andromeda is one of the closest and it looks tiny even though it's 150,000 light years on its long diameter. Even leaving here we would feel forlorn and out of breath even before we left our solar system. Nothingness, nothingness on every side. And remember, a light year is a unit of distance, not time. Travelling at 186,000 miles per second, it's the distance light travels in one year; or it's 186,000 x 60 seconds x 60 minutes x 24 hours x 365 days, or 586 billion miles and change; then multiply by the number of light years to Andromeda and you get 11.7 million trillion miles and more change, and that tells you how long our clothesline needs to be. But why? It is to be remembered by a universe that creates us from the silence of space to let us coalesce into suns and planets and seas and shores and lakes and trees and creatures that swim then crawl then climb then fly then walk, then read, then use typewriters; with lungs and hearts and limbs and . . . what for? To live then die and vanish? Is that the way the universe looks at us? I'm afraid so. You see, I don't think it really cares. I don't think it keeps score no matter what Moses and the apostle Paul and Allah tell us. I don't think the universe ever heard of us. It's a little too big and there are so many records to keep, or would be. So a clothesline is some kind of a cry to say. "Hey, look at us! See what we did! Look at the drawings I made as a child, we each made as children. I want to tell you about the time I first fell in love, the first time we all fell in love. I want to hang a Xerox copy of my first paycheck on the clothesline, the birth certificate of each of my children, a description of my wife's underwear and how much I like her when she's wearing the lavendar ones or none at all." Have you any idea universe, how wonderful this is? You know, I think the answer is "no". You don't know. You don't even understand what I'm saying. Mostly you don't even hear me - you're too far away. I want to hang a tape recorder that plays endlessly the music played at my grandmother's funeral. I want you to look at a copy of an old tintype of an uncle of mine 5 generations back standing there in his Civil War uniform his union army cap and coat, holding a rifle beside him, the butt on the ground. The Civil War - yes, so many wars. How many on this one little planet alone? Maybe 100,000? You know, universe, I think you set us up on this one, made us or our environment or both too inadequate so once in a while we went into grisly orgies of killing each other. for what? You don't know? Aren't you supposed to know? Aren't you supposed to contain all of us, our emotions, our dreams, our Gods, everything that has been created, ever created? What? I can't hear you. Our mementos on the clothesline, hung out as though to dry in the solar and ultimately stellar winds, no gravity out there, so things don't hang down, there's no down or up out there things hang down and hang up and frontwards and backwards. But mostly it's our essences out there on the clothesline, our dreams are strung out on it and since they came in our sleep maybe they never lived, or died, they just never were or always were, so when we're asleep dreaming or not, are we out there on the clothesline, hanging on or hovering nearby? Joey wants his sister's corsage from the junior prom hung out. Jerry wants his first poems written to girls in his adolescense to be recorded for immortality, because all his heart and soul went into them. Everything he ever knew he was went into them. Have you ever done more than that, universe, about anything? Eremius from the 11th century told me in a dream to get his poetry out. The poetry he thought but couldn't write becaue he lived in poverty in southern Italy and never learned to write. I want everyone to know what it's like to watch the setting full moon in the dim light of dawn on our planet, to watch a bluejay in the early morning chaparrel dart through the brush, to hear several different bird calls from a distance, to see graceful mountain ridges in that pale light above silky silent haze, to hear the city early morning hum, to show the pistol that ended my daughter's life with her own blood on her fingers and her lips, and to ask oneself what difference does it make, we all have to die sometime, ask the universe that hardly notices but let me say a death like this makes a great difference, an awful terrible difference. Once the word got out about this clothesline I've been hearing from - I mean millions, thousands, in my dreams and my imagination mostly only through me the things on the line now the sounds of the Virgin Mary's first orgasm. The dried up ear Vincent cut off, now a rich celestial source of self-regenerating gold and yellow pigment. Ruben's palette hanging on a clothespin, Rembrandt's, Goya's. Pope Urban the 4th's obscene poetry, Queen Elizabeth's thought-channeled correspondence with William Shakespeare. William the Conqueror's first tooth, Charlie Chaplin's unpublished published scripts - everything just everything my mother's sewing machine the old Victrola we played Von Suppe's Poet and Peasant overture on when I was 6 and could just peak over the top of and watch it turn. Bhutia Tensing's shoes he wore with Hilary when Tensing was the first human to scale Mt. Everest, everything everything, there's room for everything it's piling up from the ages wanting to be conscious real remembered knowing each other. And then - from the other end some tugging on the line from Andromeda. They - they? - want the same to endure as long as the unconscious universe endures but we have to participate with consciousness to tell it to be conscious, more conscious, and their signals flicker toward us along the thin filament between us that at any point along fades to nothing in the void in both directions, this filament that holds our memories our dreams and realities where all sensations are echos of themselves, held as though magnetically on this cosmic wire, this silver thread between our hearts and the hearts of Andromeda; rutile needles at the speed of light stabbing through the one great crystal of the universe, at a million times the speed of light, to relieve us of our yearning to be seen and shared, because these rutile needles bear our lives, our love of life, the wish for life a force a billion times greater than even light's love for itself with its origins in boiling stars. And now other galaxies have noticed our great loving clothesline with Andromeda and all that vast life everywhere wants to be forever the same as long as stars last - without end and so let all the kisses in the universe be remembered for the little meteors they were on one dear planet or between two separate worlds where kisses can be felt. So, from any planet to look out at the great gorgeous sculptured figure of life, shimmering and flexing with its own gratitude for the part that we who live have played and given the universe itself a living immortality. Then all the universe is lit by silver threads like parabolic elliptical sculptures, the trace of the infinite number of lines from each galaxy to every other, all these giving us the shape of life, the sight of life, of memory, of desire of time and space at last existing as a shimmering sculpture of dreams and laughter of sadness and tears of holding each other through all eternity and through the infinite space of our endless universe, now full alive with all our selves. With love and memory's immortality and even the universe that is lifeless over vast reaches yet did allow life to have its magic in the streaks of lightning on all the earths, the great hyperbolic parabolic shapes entwined with every galaxy joining everything across time and space at last. the whole universe now visible as our child the universe itself the child of our love of our capacity for love the greatest force of all after all!
Sept. 26, 1991.
BOOK I — Nature and the Universe
The Tree of Tenary
At one place in the vast Sahara is one tree - at Tenary, where ages past the earth's crust sprang one tiny leak and let water on this tiny place. And then one thousand years - one bird dropped one seed beside this pool within its meager mud, to germinate and grow to leaves and roots - to be one day a fragile tree in all this space, to be at least one guide for camel caravans across this sandy sea. We salute you, tree of Tenary! Tell us once again just how it went, just how you did all this... Then tell us where we go from here...
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
Two Chinese women
The frail Chinese lady with the cane touched the leaves of plants as she walked past - a soft look of wonder in her thin face. Her young companion in a red sweat suit walked slowly, beside her, with her hands in her pockets silently. One of them was very beautiful.
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
I remember father
(Written by someone I knew about 90 years old living in an old people's home) Let me tell you. My father was very brilliant and handsome! A charming man! If dinner was not ready when he came home, he would take his mandolin, stroll through the house playing love songs. Love songs. My mother never did have dinner ready on time.
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
Old Macedonian Woman
Macedonia's memories holding sway Over years of rhythm's joys denied. The graceful beat makes new the gaze from wrinkled eyes, The toothless smiles, with faint remembered kisses on rocky meadows, Savored long ago, though custom said A woman's passion must in silence be. All rediscovered in the dancing figures serpentining by, So close to feel the heat of motion, out of time and yet in time. Her ancestral peasant bed, receiving , giving without knowing, And then to dance with babe in arms, to give her milk to any child. To learn thereby her power over life, To make a gift of joyful light Shed from her soul on those nearby, With all the knowing echoes found in twilight's time. Her stunted dreams have called us home at last, To tell us that our age is but our youth in fuller flight, An upward, soaring cadence - without end.
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
The son of Michael Luther King, Sr.
There was nothing unusual about Martin. He was born of a Baptist preacher's wife in Atlanta in 1928, January 15 to be exact. He was born after difficult labor, a round and quiet little soul that stared at you trying to focus glazed eyes. He was like any other middle class kid in Atlanta, except that he was black, a "Negro" they said back in those days, with some Irish blood in him too. But that didn't make any difference when later he played baseball and football on the corner lot. He was a tough competitive kid, everybody knew that. Everybody picked him first when they chose up sides. I suppose they also played "war" once in a while, and there'd be a big to-do over which side would be the "Germans". It was the Great Depression, even bigger than the present one, the biggest failure of capitalism ever. Oh, sure, World War I was a failure of capitalism, but everyone worked. You didn't see hundreds standing in line in dark overcoats in the cold. But Martin's family did okay, only two generations from share-cropping. His dad pulled himself up and became a preacher and at least that gave you some kind of a living. His dad took a rundown debt-ridden Baptist church, and pumped life into it, with the sheer force of his will, and even built seven choirs in that one church. A church choir, the sound of a church choir, one of the greatest human sounds on earth. People flocked into these warming nests of emotional rhythms, these clusters of singing Teddy Bears, smiling wide, feeling fulfillment, a sanctuary from the prejudice in the streets. Martin's childhood was favored, there was money during the Depression, his father was influential, and Martin had a chance to see the power of the spoken word, how congregations could be ignited and moved to action by words shared by all of them, spoken by one person. He began to want to be such a figure, to speak for the Lord, to speak for his people. He once said to his mother, "You just wait and see. I'm going to get me some big words." And so he went through childhood, and in a display of baffling complexity, the future great Martin Luther King, Jr., attempted suicide not once but twice before he was 13 years of age. Both occasions involved his beloved grandmother, Jennie Williams, first when she was knocked unconscious by Alfred Daniel, his little brother, when that grandmother died in 1941. As Lerone Bennett, Jr., one of King's biographers says of Martin's grandfather: Part Negro and part Irish, James Albert King, the beginning, was a hard-working sharecropper who dreamed of buying a small farm for his family. But as he sank deeper and deeper into debt, he gave up hope and spent his weekends to drink himself into forgetfulness. James Albert King's soil, a soil that yielded peasants, paupers, murderers, robbers and finally Luther King, was that soil of sorrow. To work from sun-up to sun-down for a whole year and to end owing 'the man' $400 for the privilege of working to do this year after year and to sink deeper and deeper into debt; to be chained to the land by bills at the plantation store; to wash away this knowledge with bad gin, to blot it out in an ecstasy of song and prayer; to sing, to pray, to cry... The James Kings bore 10 children, one of which was Martin's father - Michael Luther King, born in 1899. His name did not become Martin Luther King until he was 22 years old - Martin, the name his father James wanted him to have, a name to become known world-wide a generation later. All the usual things happened to Martin, Jr., at adolescence exclusion from play with his white friends, at school, bright and precocious, and skipped the 9th grade, his father, growing in power in the black community received his share of threats from the Ku Klux Klan in Atlanta. Martin Jr. had his first cigarette behind a fence, a smooth talker with girls with whom he danced at every chance, and changed girlfriends like he changed the tweed suits he adored. He would "go to the grass" with peers, to settle differences by physical combat, winner take all. He was a typical, tough, bright, middle class kid, who struggled like others with being a male and being a black male. And so . . . , we know about Rosa Parks in 1955 and Montgomery, and we know about Birmingham and Selma and Atlanta and the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church and the Ebenezer Baptist Church, and Martin Luther King's ties with Ghandi, and later the Nobel Peace Prize and that ghastly motel balcony . . . in Memphis in 1968 and his incredible leadership and statesmanship in the years in between - and we also can value these words his wife Coretta chose of the hundreds of thousands he spoke, that left their mark on our understanding of the nature of power and privilege in the world that all lay on the unique foundation he learned from Ghandi - the concept of power, human power, for all of us of every race, the power based on resistance, loving resistance, but at all costs resistance, to stand tall and quiet and define yourself by your own knowledge and love for others, and your own recognition that millions love you too. Here are some of the words of her husband Martin that Coretta King chose among all the things he said in his life: he once said - As long as there is poverty in the world I can never be rich, even if I have a billion dollars. As long as diseases are rampant and millions cannot expect to live more than 30 years, I can never be totally healthy. I can never be what I ought to be until you are what you ought to be. No individual or nation can stand out boasting of being independent. We are interdependent. New laws are not enough. The emergency we now face is economic, and it is a desperate and worsening situation. For the 35 million poor people in America, there is a kind of strangulation in the air. In our society it is murder, psychologically, to deprive a man of a job or an income. You are in substance saying to that man that he has no right to exist. He said to us, when evil men plot, good men must plan. when evil men burn and bomb, good men must build and bind. when evil men shout ugly words of hatred, good men must commit themselves to the glories of love. When millions have been cheated for centuries, restitution is a costly process. Inferior education, poor housing, unemployment, inadequate health care - each is a bitter component of the oppression that has been our heritage. Each will require billions to correct. Justice so long deferred has accumulated interest and its cost for this society will be substantial. And again, the deep rumblings of discontent that we hear today is the thunder of disinherited masses, rising from dungeons of oppression to the bright hills of freedom, in one majestic chorus the rising masses singing, i n the words of our freedom song, 'Ain't gonna let nobody turn us around.' All over the world, like a fever, the freedom movement is spreading in the widest liberation in history. He reminded us, the Bible tells the thrilling story of how Moses stood in Pharaoh's court centuries ago and cried, 'Let my people go.' A true revolution of values will lay hands on the world order and say of war: "This business of burning human beings with napalm, of filling our nation's homes with orphans and widows, of injecting poisonous drugs of hate into the veins of peoples normally humane, of sending men home from dark and bloody battlefields physically handicapped and psychologically deranged, cannot be reconciled with wisdom, justice, and love. A nation that continues year after year to spend more money on military defense that on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death. He taught us, the greatest irony and tragedy of all is that our nation, which initiated so much of the revolutionary spirit of the modern world, is now cast in the mold of being an arch antirevolutionary. We are engaged in a war - the war in Vietnam - that seeks to turn the clock of history back and perpetuate white colonialism. He cried out, "we cannot remain silent as our nation engages in one of history's most cruel and senseless wars. During these days of human travail we must encourage creative dissenters. We need them because the thunder of their fearless voices will be the only sound stronger than the blasts of bombs and the clamor of war hysteria.." He sang to us, Hatred and bitterness can never cure the disease of fear; only love can do that. Hatred paralyzes life; love releases it. Hatred confuses life; love harmonizes it. Hatred darkens life; love illumines it. He said, something should remind us once more that the great things in this universe are things that we never see. You walk out at night and look up at the beautiful stars as they bedeck the heavens like singing lanterns of eternity and you think you can see all. Oh, no You can never see the law of gravitation that holds them there. Love is the most durable power in the world. This creative force, so beautifully exemplified in the life of our Christ, is the most potent instrument available in mankind's quest for peace and security. He admonishes us, the belief that God will do everything for man is as untenable as the belief that man can do everything for himself. It, too, is based on a lack of faith. We must learn that to expect God to do everything while we do nothing is not faith but superstition. Forgiveness is not an occasional act, it is a permanent attitude, he reminds us. And so, this is the giant, god-like stature of Martin Luther King, Jr., who became known world-wide and is revered everywhere as a good and brave man; who once smoked his first cigarette behind a fence, like many of us, flirted with the girls liked others his age, wondered about the meaning of life, struggled with and chose his path in the church, then found himself unexpectedly challenged and invited to live a life of greatness, one that will echo down through the next two or three centuries as one of the most precious and bravest lives ever lived on this earth.

A 2nd class Mexican bus
2 crates of broccoli across the aisle 3 chickens hanging upside down from a broomstick in the back soft faces, peaceful beautiful faces young men in white shirts not tucked in and the top buttons open straw peasant hats a voice and a guitar sing in the back 3 guys and 2 saguaros at a desert stop one has a guitar, one still peeing beside a saguaro, first water it's had in weeks on the bus everyone waits, talking and laughing everyone, including the bus driver patiently wait for the guy to finish they all know the feeling - a full bladder on a bumpy bus Next time you're in Mexico be sure to ride a 2nd class Mexican bus -- to somewhere . . . . .
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
They sit in doorways
They sit in doorways in the shady heat, in La Habana, Sao Paolo, Buenos Aires and New Orleans on hot afternoons in these cities born in the centuries. The dogs wander with mange, their ribs, their desperate faces, with stumbling steps seeking even drops of spit to lick. And yet there is great machinery to carve out factories, opera houses, marbled mansions and government buildings. And yet - they sit in doorways in the heat, the shady heat, their appealing empty faces looking our way. The dogs wander with their mange, their lost looks, their desperate steps, to find anything to lick. We have built empires, fought complete world wars, destroyed cathedrals, killed ten million babies on two continents, but they sit in doorways in the heat, the shady heat, watching us with hope and without hope. The dogs wander in the heat, their sore feet, their desperate hunger, they wander in these cities of their hell, in these cities of neglect. We send satellites to Saturn, invade tiny countries, medium countries, very tiny countries, we threaten big countries, we undermine medium large countries, we help two corporate giants fornicate and give birth to one hydraheaded cosmic corporation. They sit in doorways in the heat, the shady heat, watching us. The dogs wander in the heat, their desperate ribs, their barren furry faces, looking for a bit of food, a tiny bit of love, a tiny bit of earth, to finally sanctify those heated pavements, and those shady doorways, where they sit, here in the tropics, in the heat.
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
Lavender and orange Cesar Chavez
Cesar Chavez is gone, but he was once just like the little boy playing with two friends at the side of the dirt road. His roots are also in an older child, hungry and weary after picking grapes in the hot sun, his torn hat giving him little shelter from the San Joaquin sun. Cesar was one of the children in the Chavez family, with sisters and brothers. The Chavez family was like so many families, their origins in the Spanish language south of the border in Mexico, up here in California that once was Mexico, but was taken from them into the English-speaking world. Cesar is in every family, every Spanish-speaking hut, every Spanish-speaking group of Latinos talking softly in the shade of a tree somewhere between Fresno and Bakersfield. He will be in the laughter at weddings, the dancing at parties on Friday and Saturday nights, the sharing of food at a picnic table on Sunday afternoons. He will be present in steamy kitchens in small houses without air conditioning, the kisses at parting time between lovers, grandparents and grandchildren, both this year and on this same day a hundred years from now. He will be in the blood of his people, during their travail in a foreign land, a land that has become foreign to itself as well. He will be by the bedside with midwives, bringing new little chiquitos and chiquitas into the world. He will be there more and more in our Anglo world, as over the centuries to come, across the races and ethnic origins that so far keep us apart unless we struggle against it. Cesar Chavez will be one of the Caesars in the history books, one that Shakespeare did not write about, but may yet one day in other worlds. Cesar Chavez is an old redwood giant in our forest, a great expanse of dry land leading up to the wild hills to the southwest, he will be the lightning in gray skies, the downpour of rain in April afternoons, when the world is between hot and cold, between day and night, between life and death, as it has always been. He will be in all growing things, in the new spring grass that paints the wild areas green toward summer, in their dry parched brownness in August's heat. He will be in bird calls, in mocking birds, blue jays, crows and magpies, all living as fully as they can in their part of the world without the complexities of human life, of human survival. He will feel our lives, like his own, as he did when he lived among us. his own inadequacy, just as we feel ours, he is ultimately so like us, his hopes and labors for a better world, sometimes so lonely and tired late at night, the night before the beginning of another La Huelga pilgrimage, with one last cup of coffee before he turns out the lights and locks the door. The next 3 weeks to make history, to write a new chapter of California history between Delano and Sacramento, that the press cannot ignore no matter how it tries. Then, for the days and years to come, with the passage of the seasons we will think of him when the lavender lupines reappear like delicate blankets for a whole people. We will also think of him as the bright California poppies appear scattered in the heat of dry slopes, telling us again the forces of life are absolutely indestructible. These lavender lupines, these orange poppies, the colors of Cesar Chavez - we will keep in our memories as the seasons pass, our lavender and orange, our lavender and orange Cesar Chavez. Cesar - in his own immortal colors, so like a latter-day Cuatemoc in the gorgeous Aztec robes of long ago.
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
I am Cuban, and I still fix typewriters for the revolution
I am a simple country person. I remember the bohios and the gusanos crawling from the soil into my older sister's bare feet and through her body to her heart and liver where they devoured her life and left her on the bed staring with wide blank eyes toward the ceiling as she died. I remember the yuca root we ate three times a day, the toilet on the ground among the palms behind the bohio. I remember how I almost died of diarrhea when I was six and how Lucia and Rufino the little ones did die. I remember no electricity - ever. I remember the sugar zafra and how my father slept 3 hours a night to work those few months each year and earned $90 - for the whole zafra. I remember the fidelistas in the mountains, the Sierra Maestra and I heard of Fidel at bars in the village, how everyone hoped he and his fighters would change things the way they said they would when there was no more Batista. I remember that day at the beginning of 1959 when their columns entered Habana from Matanzas and Santa Clara, and the war was over, and how the people were wild, except the owners and the Americans. I remember the Agrarian Reform, the Urban Reform, the literacy program - I learned how to read much better. I remember the sabotage in the cane fields, the blowing up of the Belgian ship "Le Coubre" in our harbor by the CIA, at least that's what they said - all the mysterious explosions in those days. And then there was Playa Giron. I remember the school in Holguin where I began to learn - everything. And now - it is 30 years later. I am older and the Yanqui strangles us because we do not want to be owned by them. We need everything, it is hard. I had potatoes and bread for the last 5 meals. My shoes need to be fixed and I can afford it but the shoemaker has nothing. I get a pension and it is enough - just barely. But we need so much. Since I am good at fixing things, for years I fixed lamps and electric tools and typewriters. Now I am old, much older. But I am still useful. I am still a revolutionary. I fix typewriters for the revolution.

The upper class
The beautiful older woman from Venezuela, her expressive, open face, and her daughter who looks so much like her - and her son-in-law, who smiles at his wife a couple of times a day but who is basically a very handsome Latin American nincompoop with a stiff graceful slow looking straight ahead kind of military walk and his arms hanging limp and straight down, who looks like he's too distinguished to shine his shoes but doesn't object to feeling a little love for his wife or his mother-in-law when they shine them in good spirits so he'll look nice and the amazing thing is they are loving and open in such a way that they don't even notice he's basically a 12 year old nincompoop who now is 35 living in the Venezuelan nincompoop upper class.
June 13, 1991.

A hollowness in his profile
Good looking young man who looks older and worn, a discouraged slope to his shoulders, a hollowness in his profile. Short beard, looking unwashed. His eyes cast about - which way to go? He eventually crosses the street. There is no destination, no goal, because this morning he did not come from anywhere, his roots have shriveled and let him drift on the wind into the world.

The contras
The contras are poverty-stricken peasants who never learned how to read and needed a job and Gilberto told you about money and food and clothes and good shoes for once, and guns but they taught you how to use them and some priests who spoke native Spanish gave you guidance and took your confessions and told you the bible says how evil the government and the communist farms are that took land from the good people who took good wild care of the land by owning it for generations in the name of the Lord Jesus and Mary the mother of God, and at first you didn't feel good shooting other peasants with other soldiers dressed like you, but you learned you had to to save the country from the communist devils who were crucifying the Lord every day and you knew that was true because sometimes when you were resting under a tree your rosary beads spoke to you and told you to keep the faith

Old folks' home
One in a remedial chair faces the door, her face round jowels squaring the face, staring blankly; light blue blouse, necklace - no one to talk to her daughter, Connie, left a half hour ago, leaving her to think back when she and Will married then Connie was born and the church the choir, the walks in the woods, the family gatherings like yesterday. No one to talk to. Everyone is gone. Lillian pours over her bible at her desk. Always there, in profile. Her back shaped like a letter C. White hair stacked up. All day, Lillian and her bible. She knows she's old but the other night she dreamed she saw herself nude on a little beach by the lake with her first boy friend, Edgar, also nude. She woke up that night in disbelief, bewildered to be in an old people's home. She was dazed til dawn. Margaret walks up and down the halls, sometimes with her walker. Her dress hikes up in back, her beads clatter against her walker in a certain rhythm, making her think of the high school band she once was in. She laughs to herself, remembering funny stuff on TV. She had very nice breasts, once. Now? She can't do much with them. Besides, the men there are all so old and just sit in the hall leaning against the wall watching TV by the nurses' station, til they fall asleep. She'd like to write to her children, especially the oldest. What was his name? Teddy? Yes. He looks just like his dad. But Phil's been gone so long. It's hard to believe. Old Billy is 83. He lives peacefully in a lovely cloud. He never could think of death. He's in room 277, all to himself. Eleanor still wishes she could go to college. She's in 239A, a shared room. A sensitive spirit, able to feel angry at attendants when they are harsh at times.. She is my first wife and she is still bright and thoughtful and lovely and I am proud of her. Ben, everybody calls him Benny, wants to talk politics all the time. He likes the old ladies and still gets an erection when he has to go to the toilet in the mornings. He's been trying to get the world to be a better place for 60 years and he's getting disgusted, he likes Millie and Sheryl best, sort of, but he can't figure out what to do about it. And then his kids never come by, he might as well let the ladies think he's a bachelor or a widower or something but they just smile at him and go back to sleep in front of TV or have to go to the bathroom. So he switches to politics to work off steam. Then Margaret Golby, not the other one, and Arthur. Everyone smiles at their little affair. Once in a while they've sneaked a little kiss, looking sideways and they put their hands on each other's shoulder blades and everyone clicks their tongue and says 'oh my', at these goings on but it livens up the day and most of the women aren't very jealous. Billy the only other man on the wing is still in his lovely pink world and doesn't notice any of this. Of special interest is the sneaky little sight of them patting each other on the behind once in a while, mostly him patting her on the behind. Then the best of all was when Amy saw Arthur coming out of Margaret's room at 4 AM one morning, which became a very important occasion for everyone that could, to say "Oh, my goodness", and several of the women had dreams the next week or two that were sort of - well sort of erotic. But you see - if you just visited here once or twice you would think you were seeing old people, older men and women who were in decay, their lives nearly at an end, little to live for, their best years their vibrant years their sexual years far far behind. unless somehow you were able to plumb to your own lower depths and see the wondrous quality of deeper older life, and you would hear the inner youthfulness that lasts, almost to the very end.
BOOK II — Sketches of Strangers
Rivka lived
Rivka Siegel is someone you never heard of. I just barely heard of her. Wizened, looks pathetic, talks pathetic, but - but Rivka Sigel lived, served in the Israeli Army in honorable days. Drove earth moving equipment in California. Men tried to plow her under. She held on - to become a valid driver - to move the earth to move her share. Men, union men, pounding at her fingerhold and finally broke her free - a woman, whoever heard of a woman cat or roller or backhoe driver. Shit. They want everything. And so reduced to life's margins, Rivka made her back yard home for homeless ones. The place a mess, both in and out. But it was a loving home she built for lonely ones. You never heard of Rivka Sigel. I just barely heard of Rivka Sigel.

The Battle of Hastings
The Norman horsemen rushed at the Saxon foot soldiers, toward the edge of the meadow, sabers or cross bows drawn, peering through shield helmets. Aron of the Saxons, blond, sidestepped and lunged at the charging Friant, a muscled Norman dark-haired one, dear to William himself. The horse whinny-screamed as Aron's dagger struck his rib cage. Horse saliva was smeared on Aron's shoulder. Friant whirled and struck with his saber at two Saxons, Aron and another, but the blade whistled above their heads. Again Friant charged and as the horse reined up at the men, he was pitched to the ground, still gripping the handle of his saber. The rising roar and screech of the battle became deafening. Men and horses whirled charged roared screamed whinnied grunted clashed, metal fell heavily. Mon Dieu, Mien Gude, Mein Gott. Friant swung his long saber. Aron ducked the blade struck another Norman on the chest who fell heavily under another Norman horse. Aron pulled a dagger from his tunic and lunged at Friant, still the closest Norman, who was struggling to regain his balance, Aron's blade catching Friant's gloved hand, ripping the saber from his grasp. The Frenchman jerked his own dirk from his mailed loincloth and stood facing Aron, arms held wide. Both were in battle-poise, daggers drawn. Aron dropped his dagger and pulled his short-handled axe from his belt behind. All England was in the balance, arrows flew, sabers clashed, men lay groaning in blood on every side. Aron and Friant lunged and stabbed, whirled and gripped eath other, seizing the other's weapon wrist. The power of Norman France, Normandy, England, Hastings. Aron and Friant, arms wrestled trembling overhead, empires in blood and sabers, courage fear death and hideous wounds, spurting blood from men and horses. Friant jerked suddenly free and plunged his dirk into Aron's middle, who brought his short axe suddenly down in his recoiling agony and it plunged into Friant's neck, a severed ear hanging swinging, as blood spurted. and Aron's own torn abdomen, his clothing now warm and sticky with blood. Empire with terrible fear. Oh mon dieu. Oh, God. I'm dying, finish me off, they crawled toward each other. Horses careening close by, they reached to finish the kill, their fingers clawed at the other's face. Their bodies moved so little now. Both lay, close by, almost as though in rest after some dread and unforgettable ecstasy. The battle of Hastings, was fought the rest of that day, October 14, 1066, with screams and steel, blood and brains, terror and triumph, empire and the silence of defeat that lasts until both the winners and losers merge after a thousand years into the same society and language, with no one living who knew or honored those other Saxons or Normans on that other day so long ago, or ever knew the names of Aron, the Saxon, or Friant, the Norman . . .
BOOK III — I Am Writing of Handgrenades, Butterflies and Kisses
Wounded knee
was an intersection between two worlds, two geologic epochs, two lightning storms, two rivers, two tectonic plates in human history, two men, one wise native chief, one illiterate white man. It ended the last community of Lakota in the wilds, the last 200 women and children and a few warriors. The great geologic divide between open plains, steep crags in the alpine glow at sundown, fish leaping in rapids to spawn, gently-grazing horses of the Sioux, the Lakota, and on the other side, the complete surrender of life to machinery, to electricity, to roaring engines and smashing horrifying drop hammers. The divide is across a gulf, a lacuna, that mankind had to create a route across, a fracturing of all calendars and rosetta stones. Wounded Knee was between the Paleozoic and Mezozoic eras in human history, between simple processes beside rivers and in the shade of fruit-bearingf trees, and the huge iron-clad rectangular-scaled reptiles, showing how progress can be hideous. Wounded Knee occurred between two lightning storms, during the inky blackness between bolts, so living creatures would not see the ugliness of power, of the consequences flaming in the night, and scorching the grasslands where the buffalo stood in herds, and native children looked toward the mountains with wonder. Wounded Knee was healed in former years by its caressing in river waters, to excite circulation in icy winters, to breathe fresh life in warmer summer water. Wounded Knee is a symbol for all the invasions of the white man, bringing with him all the maladies of modern life, including rifles to kill those of different colors. Tectonic plates merged on the eastern slopes of the great mountain chain that wrinkled up a hundred million years ago, that showed across the plains the beauty of snowy crags, for all the tribes to be guided by, toward places of safety throughout the seasons. Yet the tragic end was born of a redneck Indian agent, who knew only anger and fear and ignorance, and who wired Washington that the sacred ghost dances of the Lakota were war dances and had to be crushed, stamped out, killed if necessary, to we could go west across the horizon where millions of acres of mineral ores and buffalo and ownership of land, ownership of forests and mountains, and peaks and glaciers and deserts and wild life we could hunt down and slaughter for furs and redneck trophies, all in the service of beautiful murderous conquest -- all this became Wounded Knee in our history, that someday through magic and wildlife dreams and the whispers of clouds and the murmer of cold mountain streams will be seen as the hideous murders of Lakota of every age, even babies in their papoose carriers, but for now, the story must be mistold, for at least two centuries, so we can get on with murders of villages, cities, neighborhoods and farmland and wild deer and wild salmon and wild spirits of the dead of our own kind, before World Wars III and IV and World War V have come and gone, long before the sun burns itself out. . . .
November 10, 1999
BOOK III — I Am Writing of Handgrenades, Butterflies and Kisses
HIROSHIMA
Such ancient agriculture nestling in the hills. Old houses, old peasant men, women already in the fields. Ground moisture in the glades, green with rice planting. The air hazy hot under the pale sky. Today is August 6, 1962 in Hiroshima. Breakfast in Hiroshima; tomato juice, ham, pancakes, Log Cabin Syrup. How unexpected - Log Cabin Syrup - a uniquely American thing in this city. Outside the crowd gathers. The memorial crowd is quiet in Hiroshima. Today is August 6, 1945 in Hiroshima. The all clear sounds, after a restless, fitful night; Alarms rudely shaking sleep's cradle. Today Hiroshima is safe, the B-29s droned on to other targets. August 6th - Monday - a new week begins. So tired; God, to be so tired. Hiroshima stirs, figures drift back from the sheltering hills. Eight o'clock; women and children eating in the huts, in the dark lean-tos. The streets full of people; bicycles and cars, wagons and carts circling down narrow streets. The crowd grew, the children's chorus sings memorial music... A hundred boys and girls - in yellow berets. Very warm, bits of pale clouds, masses of heat clouds on the horizon. The memorial crowd is quiet, in Hiroshima. Very warm. Is every August 6th this warm in Hiroshima? Narrow shops on narrow streets, proprieters perspiring. Sultry huts... no ventilation Wreathes of flowers are placed on the memorial...the memorial music... somber, haunting. The city hums. More wreathes, one by one. Liz puts a wreath on for the Americans. Three B-29s appear out of the pale southeast. The people of Hiroshima ignore the planes. They're used to lone planes, or twos, or threes. It's the big raids they fear. Speeches now. "We hope that all the peoples on this earth will..." The B-29s move gracefully over Hiroshima. Nearly overhead. Something drops, a parachute opens, swinging gently down, ever so gently. Hundreds of doves sweep overhead, released as symbols of peace. The object is within sight. The doves circle. "...that all the peoples on this earth will find ways to live... "FLASH! 8:15! White! Pikadon! White Everyone! JESUS WHITE! BUDDHA WHITE! Evaporate! Gone! Gone! Gone. The memorial gong... 8:15. 40,000 people pay their devotion The clouds seem in attendance... on all sides. The memorial crowd is quiet, in Hiroshima. The screaming, everywhere pieces of human beings claw their way... Clothed in hanging rags of skin, Sizzling fat on open flesh. Children and babies underfoot like crisp bacon. Blind Japanese, some with eyeballs hanging... Stumbling over half-living children. The heat! The heat! Suddenly day is night, The sun a bloody disc in boiling darkness... The execution of 200,000 human beings; with care and method; the 'target' - Hiroshima, history's greatest gas oven. How unexpected, a uniquely American thing in this city... A uniquely American thing. The memorial crowd is quiet - in Hiroshima.

Burger King
(As many already know, the fast food chains get their beef from other, cheaper places in the world; for example, Central America, where land and labor are cheaper, but to graze cattle you must clear rainforests.) A hamburger for $2.50 is very special at Burger King, for in it are azure blue butterflies, tomatoes, giant cicadas, onions, bits of jaguars and anacondas twenty feet long, great lilies and wild orchids, Some beef, a few Venus fly traps, and 8000 species that haven't been catalogued; including the mold on the Alarana berries in the rainforests of Panama that would have been the cure for cancer had we found it in time.... Then add some ground up laughing monkeys and lavender parrots, for a little variety. The land was cleared to graze for beef for 10 years until the soil erodes and has no nourishment in Costa Rica. But never mind, there's always Venezuela and Brazil, and eventually Canada and California. So, for now..... just put a little more mustard on, maybe it will cover up the funny taste.

The third cross
The third cross tells it all. It says the Christian crusades are in your front yard, are in your town, and that you got to go. You're black or dark or aboriginal and you got to go. Remember your daddy 15 years ago. After the third cross he got tarred and feathered by the Christian crusade to keep holiness and the bible and heaven clean and nice clear white, cause that's what the Ku Klux preachers said the bible said. Your daddy, after 2 months he was still getting little patches of tar off, some with little itchy pieces of chicken feathers. Then they tell of 6 little girls hiding under mother's hoop skirt while the Klan circled like executioners because your daddy was Seminole in a town on a continent where he didn't belong but where he'd been ten thousand years and that awful night when daddy was maybe dying and mama hitched up the mules in the rain and tried to get all of us to the doctor in town for daddy and luck was with us for once when we got across the bridge with the mules about 7 minutes before the wild creek washed it down river. Maybe it was the white dove we saw in the bridge rafters, that maybe was God for a little while. Then the doctor came the next morning to the machine shop on the edge of town where you all had to hide soaking wet and somebody maybe the white dove brought some food and old Doc Morrissey said he had good news and bad news. Tell me the good news first mama said, and Doc said well he doesn't have typhoid, that's the good news but they burned your house down to the ground only the pot belly stove's still there, that's the bad news - all in the rain. Where, where dear Lord was your white dove? Take this nightmare cross from us tonight, this third cross stabbed in the earth before our little place on the earth. God have mercy, let these crusades pass, let these circling Christian murderers pass, these nightmares dressed in white who are our neighbors who hate us because Bill is Seminole, because he's been here 10,000 years. Oh, white dove, help us, let us have peace and mercy white dove, please sit on the third cross and put a spell on it so it sinks into the earth, into its own everlasting grave, never again to let third hooded crosses circle the ruins of our home, the shelter of our 6 little sisters who live with us, and let the white dove bless them to still be able to love and share laughter when the're grown women, and will never, ever again see or have to think of a third cross stabbed in the earth.

"Troops pass atomic test"
(Title from a newspaper clipping — S.F. News, Monday, June 2, 1952: "Troops pass atomic test, / Can attack safely after A-Bomb blast.") Yes, they passed the test, they could attack into the high radiation zone without effect. The effects wouldn't appear until 20 years had passed and hair had fallen out of half their heads and one third had liver cancer, 40% had lymphoma, a fourth had prostate, rectal, foreskin or brain cancer. They would be okay. Only 74% would die before they were 60. Not bad considering the stakes the word is always attack. There's always somebody with a big stick, a big gun, a big dick, and they want everything possible The word is "attack." The troops passed the test, that day at least. It was on a Sunday, the day of our Lord, the day of the nuclear Lord, June 1, 1952. Not a single soldier had a single problem during June. Only a few problems showed up in July, just minor skin lesions, or dizziness or vomiting, aspirin could fix easy. Troops pass atomic test. They can attack. No problem. World War III will be over by the time we're covered with skin lesions and they'll be all healed before World War IV, and by then it'll all be over because we'll own everything and pay wages to Asia and Africa and Latin America and we'll have all the surplus and we'll always be able to attack with nuclear cannisters and cash registers and stock certificates cancer and the troops pass atomic test attack attack skin cancer breast cancer attack attack bone cancer, the troops pass atomic test with no visible damage so every day of every week because now we know the troops will be American and they'll be able to pass the atomic test pass the atomic test. So . . . , you pacifists, we're running this show, and we know what we're doin'. You'll see the troops are passed they're all passed they've all passed and we still attack right up to the end - "The troops pass atomic test."
BOOK III — I Am Writing of Handgrenades, Butterflies and Kisses
A Revolution is..... Nicaragua is......
It is a boy who looks 6 but says he's l0 Nicaragua is brown Maya faces in repose, and can read my watch. A revolution is a skinny horse, It is two 20-year-olds in fatigues that return a smile easily, clear eyes, lips steady and full, rifles slung carelessly. Nicaragua is a crowded bus with 3 kids on the back and 6 on top. A revolution is 5 children staring at you, It is 3 pigs crossing the road but we miss them. It is a 45-year-old pregnant wife at a country stop. Nicaragua is a dark rustic store with one light bulb; It is bullet holes in the Bella Peluquería, the Supermercado around the corner, in the Santa Victoria Catholic church, the Union Ferretería, the city hall and Senora Guiterrez' Panadería. The revolution is gray patch marks on the city hall from the day the national guard shot it up eight years ago. A revolution is good guys and bad guys and sometimes you couldn't tell the difference. It is a gravel road with potholes where before there was no road at all. It is 9 mothers in front of the public building with pictures of their missing sons and daughters, missing since long before the revolution. Nicaragua is a cross on the highway where Jaime didn't see the truck coming. The revolution is running water in the village for the first time. It's old Miguel laughing a toothless laugh when Maria tries to teach him to spell "casa". The revolution is pulling guard duty from midnight to dawn so the contras can't dynamite the rice storage; It's pulling guard duty so the contras won't kill the volunteers picking coffee; It's pulling guard duty so maybe you can ward off air or sea strikes by the CIA on the oil storage docks; It's pulling guard duty at the bridge they blew up last April that was fixed within a week; It's pulling guard duty when there is more useful work to be done; It's getting tired of pulling guard duty but you know you have to. The revolution is no kids starving - anywhere. It's being able to buy school clothes for the children. It's a new school for the village or the barrio, It's a new health clinic for the village or the barrio. Nicaragua is l7 people in the back of a pickup truck. It's a beloved revolutionary priest who lives and stands with the poor. It's people standing on the highway even in the dark waiting for a bus that won't have room for them but they'll get on anyway. Nicaragua is painting things different colors just for the hell of it. It's the church mural of Jesus as an Indian youth crucified in hands and feet and stabbed in the side. It's young people running the country and making mistakes and what did you expect - it was all so new and enemies were on every hand bought and paid for by the U.S. that knew everything and knew nothing needed changing. It's 3 guys pushing a car that won't start. Nicaragua is everyone returning your smile - everyone. Nicaragua is the U.S. having to run everything in Latin America - in its own "national interest". Nicaragua is some East German trucks because they needed some kind of trucks and the U.S. had embargoed this poverty-stricken country because it was Marxist or something. It's Antonio with his kids in the army truck he's driving to Corinto. It's armed campesinos that can't even spell socialism or capitalism. It's salsa dancing in every barrio on Saturday night. Nicaragua is nobody with much money, but plenty of friends. The revolution was 50,000 who died fighting the National Guard. The revolution is kids with balloons filling the front seat of the army truck they had to buy half way around the world, though the balloons and some bubblegum were smuggled through the U.S. embargo. Nicaragua is Raoul complaining about his kidneys and his low wages - maybe a good urologist could give him a revolutionary attitude. It's 2 or 3 beggars in Leon instead of two or three hundred in Leon back under Somoza. Nicaragua is having the money for a service and a party for the whole barrio to remember "Abuela" Magdalena at the time of her death; we all knew the unbelievable chances she took to get food to the rebels in the war against Somoza. Nicaragua is bongo drums, guitars, and a marimba at a mass, touching both the Catholic God and the Revolution. It's having a TV set on your block and something worth watching on it. The revolution is being able to make love in privacy in your own little house. It's being able to question the doctor because you know a little something too. The "Revolution" is being in "Nicaragua", both the way it is and the way it was. The Revolution is being... The Revolution is being proud... proud that you are a "Nicaraguan", grateful that you're there to live out the achievements of your people, to have more time to laugh, to sing, to grow old, with those you love, and with those you have learned to love....
